length_policy.policy: Target 1200 words per scene, 4800 per chapter, approximately 14400 overall. Develop lived action, choices and resistance. Never reach length by repeating information or padding imagery.

title: The Fire Beneath the Bronze
retrieval_query: Iliad heroic honor divine gift competing authority mortal vulnerability supplication war
genre: Mythic war epic; tragic alternate Trojan continuity
reader_experience: Wonder, anticipation, competing loyalties, martial terror and a costly local victory that opens a larger epic.
pov: Third-person past-tense epic narrator, with a primary focal character per scene. The narrator may supply another character’s history or inner attention in a clearly separated paragraph, but this never grants other characters private knowledge. No dialogue, quoted speech, first-person narrator, invocation or direct address. Narrate offers and commitments briefly and show their consequences.
tone_mood: Grave and martial, with tenderness in concrete duties; wonder before divine craft and unease beneath victory. No modern sarcasm or action-film triumphalism.
sensory_detail: Concrete material detail perceived through ancient experience: bronze, sea, wool, ash, labor, bodies and weather.
ending_tendency: Resolve acquisition and first deployment, not the Trojan War. End on a concrete changed obligation, not a moral summary.
premise: After nine years before Troy, with Hector and Achilles alive, a mortal smith and Odysseus discover a damaged object of divine craft. Write a large, developed three-chapter opening movement, twelve scenes of approximately 1200 words each. Chapter 1 earns the discovery, difficult journey and costly acquisition of exactly six finite weapons from a hidden workshop of Hephaestus. Chapter 2 develops transport, physical trial and the coalition struggle over custody, honor and dangerous labor. Chapter 3 follows limited deployment through a contested position, an established failure, personal exposure and a costly local Greek victory. Troy does not fall. The price of divine assistance becomes a concrete new obligation. Pure third-person past-tense narration, no dialogue or quoted speech, no invocation. Homeric social imagination and material causality, not a modern military adventure. Dramatize decisions and consequences rather than expanding a synopsis.

style.register: Concrete, grave, musical ancient epic in intelligible English. Use material acts, reciprocal obligation, shame and rank; no stock modern cinematic gestures.
wording: Recurring epithets at meaningful moments; avoid attaching one to every name.
Period-fitting names: unfamiliar iron object, then iron tubes or fire-bearing tubes; keep naming consistent. No modern military vocabulary.
Ancient measures and experiences; no modern technical or psychological vocabulary.
Contemporary English grammar shaped by ancient epic; no indiscriminate thee/thou or faux-biblical filler.
Gods and human motives intertwine, while choices retain consequences.
No quotation or close reproduction of a modern translation.

figurative_language.guidance: Roughly one extended comparison per scene when earned, no mandatory quota. Let its image develop before returning to action. No modern image domains or continuous ornament.

style.interiority: Selective focalized thought tied to a practical choice, remembered obligation or fear of a specific loss; no abstract emotional labels.
style.dialogue: Forbidden: no direct or quoted speech. Do not turn speeches into repetitive reported explanations.
style.explanation: Cut explanations that merely restate legible action. Preserve purposeful epic repetition, ceremonial speech, lyricism and similes.

world_rules: Hephaestus made the weapons for a divine purpose. A particular grievance and bargain explain access; no arbitrary delivery from the sky.
Scene 1 provides only an anomalous damaged object and grounds for an expedition: NO usable gun, possession, demonstration or battlefield firing.
Scene 2 must earn the cache through an on-page journey, resistance, bargain and physical transport. The keeper has a motive beyond exposition.
Cache: exactly six cumbersome single-shot weapons, with a finite supply of prepared charges explicitly fixed at acquisition. No resupply or reproduction within this arc.
Deliberate preparation, smoke, noise, imperfect aim and wet-weather failures limit use. Possession does not guarantee a hit or victory.
Describe operation only enough to understand action and failure. Omit construction recipes and technical instructions.
No modern industry, tactical jargon, technical units or modern worldview. Men interpret unfamiliar craft through their ancient experience.
Divine aid never grants perfect knowledge, unlimited supplies or immunity. A god cannot retroactively cancel an established cost.
Odysseus accepts an obligation to restore a neglected sacred trust and acknowledge the maker. Specify a future concrete vulnerability; no gratuitous sacrifice of an innocent.
Agamemnon claims the cache but depends on skilled men and coalition consent. Achilles cannot be silenced by invoking the common cause.
Trojans observe, infer and adapt plausibly; no instant knowledge of operation or inventory.
Track each weapon, custodian, condition, remaining charges, travel, wounds, witnessed facts and private bargains.
End in a costly local Greek success, NOT Troy’s fall. Hector and Achilles survive; larger political and divine conflicts remain open.

initial_facts.text: After nine years, the Achaean coalition remains outside Troy; Hector and Achilles live. No Greek possesses or understands the unfamiliar weapons at the opening.
Thestor seeks wages and passage for his surviving apprentice. He is a mortal smith, not master of divine craft.
Agamemnon commands a coalition of rival lords; Achilles and he have strained relations over honor.

chapter_contract.arc: A household attempt to leave the war becomes a divine debt and a new dependence on indispensable labor. The first victory must worsen that dependence.
causal_spine: Discovery earns a risky journey, not a weapon.
A difficult approach and a resisted bargain earn possession. Fix six weapons and the exact charge count here.
A physical trial establishes both power and failure before rival lords impose conditions.
The established failure forces Achilles to expose himself; success costs someone something already valued.
chapter_contract.continuity: Each scene begins after the previous irreversible choice. Track possession, usable charges, weather, travel, injury and who witnessed what. Do not restage a bargain or discovery.
chapter_contract.ending: A concrete demand on labor, protection or restitution closes the opening movement. Troy remains unconquered; Hector and Achilles live.

quality_contract: Third person, past tense, no dialogue or quoted speech, no invocation, no scene headings.
Every decisive event unfolds through attempted action, resistance, a credible alternative and an irreversible choice. Avoid plot-summary transitions at the moments that matter.

Thestor pursues household departure through competent work; his usefulness gives powerful men reason to prevent it. Odysseus solves a present problem by accepting a future vulnerability. Achilles must embody the danger he argues about.
Use close material perception and ancient social obligations. Do not label every emotion, explain an image twice, or repeat stock eyes, hands, weight and measured voices.
An epic simile must illuminate the current physical predicament and return cleanly to action. Elevated language is neither faux-archaic filler nor a translation imitation.
No repeated paragraphs, recycled bargaining, retroactive costs, unearned knowledge, instantaneous transport or offstage solutions.
Chapter revision must preserve the sequence and strengthen setup/payoff across scene boundaries; memory is extracted only after revisions.
chapter_arcs: The household seeks departure; discovery traps its skilled labor in a difficult journey. End with a binding bargain and physical transfer of a finite cache, not a battle.
Bring the cache home under real constraints. Test it, expose limits, struggle over custody and authority, then commit to a limited deployment under a credible deadline.

Move the operators into danger. Let partial success expose a limitation already tested. Achilles must choose personal exposure; Hector observes and adapts. Secure a local position at irreversible cost, then enact the first concrete demand of the divine bargain.
